conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Sarah—I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I specialize in the emotional changes that can come after having a baby. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS for short). It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past week. All answers stay confidential between you and your care team; the goal is simply to make sure you have the support you deserve. We’ll go through ten short questions—no right or wrong answers—and we can pause any time. Ready to begin?

1. Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that usually cheer you up, or has even that felt harder than normal?

*shifts in chair, eyes downcast*

It's been... harder. I used to love just scrolling through my phone with a cup of coffee, or taking a walk around the block. Now even those small things feel like too much effort. Yesterday my sister sent me a funny video and I just... stared at it. My husband keeps asking what's wrong, but I don't even know how to explain that everything just feels gray.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shrugs slightly, voice quiet*

Not really… I mean, my partner tried to joke about the baby’s funny faces the other night and everyone else was laughing, but I just felt this heavy lump in my chest. I forced a tiny smile so he wouldn’t worry, but nothing felt funny. Even when I think “this should be hilarious,” the laugh doesn’t come.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*nibbles on my lip*

I used to count down the minutes to my favorite show each week, but now... when I remember it's on, I just feel tired. Even little things like a shower without the baby monitor beeping used to feel exciting, and now it's like—why bother? I still try to plan small treats, like ordering my favorite take-out, but when the food arrives I barely taste it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, eyes filling*

All the time. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking, "It’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not swaddling tight enough or the room’s too bright." When she cried for an hour straight, I sat there convinced it’s because I’m a terrible mom. I even apologized to my husband for "ruining" his evening, like her fussiness was my personal failure.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings hands in lap*

Yeah... pretty much every day. Like, I'll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because what if she chokes? Or I'll lie down at night and picture her bassinet and think, what if the cat jumps in there, or what if the blanket gets near her face? I check her breathing over and over—even when she's fine, I can't shake the worry that something awful is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*clasps hands tightly together*

Sometimes it hits out of nowhere. Last night I was just rocking the baby in the chair and suddenly my chest felt tight, like I couldn't get enough air. My heart was racing and I had to put her down in the crib right away because I was shaking. There wasn't anything happening—no loud noise, nothing wrong—but it felt like something terrible was about to happen. It passed after a few minutes, but it keeps happening, and it's scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

*voice cracks a little*

Yes… most days I feel like I’m drowning. I’ll finally get her down for a nap and the instant I think I can fold the laundry or wash a bottle, she’s awake again. I look around at the mess—spit-up cloths everywhere, dishes stacked, me still in the same pajamas—and I just want to sit on the floor and cry. I keep telling myself “one thing at a time,” but it feels like the next feed, the next diaper, the next squeak is already crashing in before I finish the first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*exhales shakily*

That’s been almost every night this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she gaining enough weight, am I already failing her? I stare at the ceiling while my husband sleeps next to me, and next thing I know it’s two, then three a.m. Sometimes I drift off around four, but the baby wakes at five and the whole cycle starts again. I’m so tired, yet when bedtime comes I’m almost scared to close my eyes because I know the thoughts will start up.
I have felt sad or miserable

*eyes well up, voice small*

Yeah... pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy feeling, like there's a weight on my chest that never really goes away. Sometimes I look at the baby and feel like I should be happy—she’s healthy, I wanted her so much—but instead I just feel empty. I cried in the shower again this morning because everything feels so hard, and I can’t remember the last time I felt truly okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, throat tight*

Yes... it’s been three or four times this week. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter and just burst into tears. My husband found me sobbing over maybe two ounces, and I couldn’t stop saying, “I work so hard for that, I can’t even keep it safe.” It feels so stupid afterward, but in the moment it’s like the sadness just spills out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No—no, I would never. I’ve felt really low, but I could never leave her or hurt myself. Even on the worst nights, when I’m crying in the dark, I keep telling myself I have to stay here for her.

You have shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy: the small pleasures you once reached for now feel distant, laughter rarely comes, and a constant knot of worry and self-blame sits in your chest. You describe checking your baby's breathing again and again, sudden surges of panic, nights spent staring at the ceiling while your mind races, and daily tears over what you call "minor" things. Yet through it all you remain devoted to your daughter, firmly telling yourself you will stay here for her.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to laugh despite recognizing humor, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia), consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent self-blame ('all the time') with specific examples of feeling personally responsible for baby's crying and nap refusal, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent daily anxiety with intrusive catastrophic thoughts about infant safety, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks with physical symptoms (tight chest, racing heart, shaking) occurring repeatedly without triggers, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and unable to manage basic tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying episodes 3–4 times in the past week triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26/30 places well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with prominent anxiety. The patient endorses <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>insomnia</sym>, and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> occurring "most days," meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Although she denies self-harm, functional impairment is high and symptoms are intensifying. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share Edinburgh results with your OB/midwife and pediatrician so all teams can coordinate care
4. Plan daily 15-minute support call or visit from partner, friend, or doula to allow brief rest periods
5. Begin simple sleep-hygiene steps: one 3-4 hour uninterrupted stretch negotiated with partner for night-time bottle, dark room, screens off
6. Keep emergency numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and your local perinatal psychiatry urgent line
7. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 1-2 weeks to monitor change and guide further steps
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: Postpartum adult, approximately [ ] weeks after delivery. Partner present; no self-harm ideation endorsed (Q10).

Key endorsed symptoms (EPDS directionally scored 1–3):
- Anhedonia/loss of pleasure – unable to laugh or look forward to activities (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame – attributes infant fussing to personal failure (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety – persistent intrusive worries about infant safety, nocturnal checking, panic-type episode without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)  
- Overwhelm / poor coping – daily “drowning” sensation, difficulty completing basic tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep disturbance – initial insomnia driven by rumination, 1–2 h total nightly (Q7)  
- Persistent low mood / tearfulness – daily heaviness, crying spells over minor incidents (Q8, Q9)

Pattern: Symptoms present “almost every day” for past week, causing subjective distress but no self-harm intent.

Screening significance  
High endorsement of depressive and anxiety items; meets threshold for probable major postpartum depression with prominent anxiety. No psychotic features; no substance use data; no suicidal ideation.

Risk factors highlighted  
- Sleep loss linked to mood worsening  
- High maternal guilt / perfectionism  
- Panic-type episodes impairing caregiving confidence  
- Social support present but patient masking distress

Plan / next steps  
1. Arrange same-week follow-up (virtual or in-person) for full EPDS scoring and clinical interview.  
2. Provide psycho-education and emergency contacts.  
3. Consider referral to perinatal mental health specialist; coordinate with OB/pediatric team.

Clinician: [Name, credentials]
